questions.question: A halfspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a set such as $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$ (or with $\geq$, $<$, $>$), where $b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Why is $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ excluded from this definition?
options: For $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ the set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{0}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$ is not convex, so the convexity results would fail.
For $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ the condition reads $0\leq b$, which never holds, so the set would always be empty.
For $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ the set is all of $\mathbb{R}^n$ or empty, so no hyperplane cuts $\mathbb{R}^n$ into two sides.
For $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ the set is neither open nor closed, so the topological results would fail.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$, $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$ and $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$. Drawn from a point of $H$, in which direction does the normal vector $\boldsymbol{a}$ point?
options: Out of $S$, into the side where $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}>b$.
Along $H$, so it points into neither side.
Out of $S$ when $b>0$ and into $S$ when $b<0$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$. Which argument proves that $S$ is convex?
options: $S$ is closed, as the preimage of $(-\infty,b]$, and closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are convex.
The map $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ is continuous, and preimages of intervals under continuous maps are convex.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $n\geq1$. Which statement about the closed halfspace $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$, with boundary hyperplane $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$, is correct?
options: $S$ is unbounded, so not compact: it contains $\boldsymbol{x}_0-t\boldsymbol{a}$ for $\boldsymbol{x}_0\in H$, $t>0$.
$S$ is compact, because it is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and contains its boundary $H$.
For $n=1$, $S$ is a closed bounded interval of $\mathbb{R}$, so in that case it is compact.
$S$ is bounded, because all of its points lie on the same side of its boundary hyperplane $H$.

questions.question: A halfspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$ (or with $\geq$, $<$, $>$) with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which of the following subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a halfspace?
Let $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon 2x_1-x_2+3x_3\leq5\}$. Which of the following points lies in $S$?
Which of the following sets equals the halfspace $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon 3x_1-x_2\geq6\}$?

The strict halfspace $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^4\colon x_1-3x_3<2\}$ is written as $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}<b\}$ with $b=2$. Which vector is the normal vector $\boldsymbol{a}$?
In $\mathbb{R}^2$, which set is the closed halfspace whose boundary is the line through $(3,0)$ and $(0,2)$ and which contains the origin?

Let $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$, $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$ and $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$. What are the interior $\operatorname{Int}(S)$ and the boundary $\partial S$?
options: $\operatorname{Int}(S)=S$ and $\partial S=H$, because $S$ is closed and contains $H$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$. Which statement about $H$ and the halfspaces with normal vector $\boldsymbol{a}$ is correct?
options: $H=\{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}\cap\{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq b\}$, and $H$ has no interior points.
$H$ is closed and convex, so like every nonempty convex set it has interior points.
$H$ is itself a closed halfspace, being a level set of $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$. Which of the following describes the complement $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus S$?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}>b\}$, an open set that is not convex.

questions.question: Let $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon 2x_1-x_2+2x_3\leq3\}$ with normal vector $\boldsymbol{a}=(2,-1,2)$, and let $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,1,1)$. For which real numbers $t$ does $\boldsymbol{p}+t\boldsymbol{a}$ lie in $S$?
The set $T=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon |x_1-x_2|\leq1\}$ is a strip between two parallel lines. How can $T$ be written in terms of closed halfspaces?
options: $T=\{x_1-x_2\leq1\}\cup\{x_1-x_2\geq-1\}$, a union of two closed halfspaces.
$T=\{x_1-x_2\leq1\}\cap\{-x_1+x_2\leq1\}$, an intersection of two closed halfspaces.
$T=\{x_1-x_2\leq1\}\cap\{x_1-x_2\leq-1\}$, an intersection of two closed halfspaces.
$T=\{x_1-x_2\leq1\}\cap\{x_1-x_2\geq1\}$, an intersection of two closed halfspaces.

questions.question: Which set is the closed halfspace in $\mathbb{R}^3$ whose boundary hyperplane passes through $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,-1,2)$ and has normal vector $\boldsymbol{a}=(2,-1,3)$, and which lies on the side that $\boldsymbol{a}$ points away from?

Let $n\geq2$, $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$, $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$, $\boldsymbol{x}_0\in S$ with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}_0=b$, and $\boldsymbol{d}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which condition on $\boldsymbol{d}$ is necessary and sufficient for $\boldsymbol{x}_0+t\boldsymbol{d}\in S$ for all $t\geq0$?

Let $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $U=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}<b\}$. Which argument correctly proves that $U$ is an open set?
options: $U$ is the complement of the closed halfspace $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b\}$, and complements of closed sets are open.
$U$ is the preimage of the open set $(-\infty,b)$ under the continuous map $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$.
The continuous map $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ sends $U$ onto the open interval $(-\infty,b)$, so $U$ is open.
$U$ does not meet the hyperplane $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b$, and a set that misses a hyperplane is open.

questions.question: Let $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2\leq4\}$. Which of the following closed halfspaces contains $S$ as a subset?

Let $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon 3x_1+4x_2\leq12\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(-1,1)$. What is the largest radius $r$ such that the closed ball $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\lVert\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p}\rVert\leq r\}$ is contained in $S$?
